[0m[38;2;80;80;80m[48;2;55;55;55m❯ Without using any tools, reply with 60 numbered lines; each line must be one long sentence of roughly 200 characters about clouds and weather. Do not read or modify any files.[0m[48;2;55;55;55m     [0m
      turbulence and strong vertical wind shear.
  37. A rainbow appears when sunlight enters falling raindrops, bends, reflects off the back of each drop, and splits into its component colors, which is why you always see one with
      the sun located directly behind you.
  38. Orographic clouds form when moist air is forced upward by mountains, cooling as it rises and condensing into clouds on the windward slopes, while the leeward side often remains
      dry in what is called a rain shadow.
  39. The global water cycle depends on clouds to move enormous quantities of water from oceans to continents, where precipitation replenishes rivers, lakes, and groundwater before
      the water eventually returns to the sea.
  40. Pileus clouds are smooth, delicate caps that briefly form atop rapidly rising cumulus towers, created when a strong updraft pushes a layer of moist air upward until it cools
      just enough to condense into a thin veil.
  41. Cold fronts usually move faster than warm fronts and bring abrupt changes, such as a narrow line of strong storms followed by clearing skies, falling temperatures, gusty winds,
      and noticeably drier air behind them.
  42. Climate scientists study clouds intensely because they both reflect sunlight back to space and trap heat near the surface, and small changes in cloud cover could significantly
      amplify or dampen future global warming.
  43. Fair-weather cumulus clouds tend to have flat bases at a consistent height, marking the level where rising air cools to its dew point, so a field of them can look like boats
      floating on an invisible, glassy lake.
  44. Graupel consists of soft, small pellets that form when supercooled droplets freeze onto falling snowflakes, and its appearance often hints that a cloud contains strong vertical
      motion and abundant liquid water at height.
  45. Doppler radar lets meteorologists see not only where precipitation is falling but also how it is moving, revealing rotation inside thunderstorms that can provide critical
      minutes of warning before a tornado forms.
  46. Asperitas clouds display a chaotic, rippling underside that resembles a rough sea viewed from below, and they were officially recognized as a distinct cloud feature by the
      World Meteorological Organization in 2017.
  47. Sea breezes develop on sunny afternoons when the land heats faster than nearby water, drawing cooler marine air inland and often triggering a line of cumulus clouds or even
      thunderstorms along the advancing boundary.
  48. Overcast winter skies can feel especially gloomy at high latitudes, where low stratocumulus decks may persist for days, blocking the weak sunshine and keeping temperatures
      steady but rarely letting any blue sky through.
  49. The anvil shape at the top of a mature thunderstorm forms when rising air reaches the stable tropopause and can no longer climb, spreading outward horizontally and carrying ice
      crystals many kilometers downwind.
  50. Ancient civilizations read the clouds for omens and practical guidance, and many traditional weather sayings, such as red sky at night bringing sailors delight, contain a
      genuine kernel of meteorological truth.
  51. Fallstreak holes, sometimes called hole-punch clouds, appear when part of a layer of supercooled droplets suddenly freezes, often triggered by a passing aircraft, and the
      resulting ice crystals fall away leaving a gap.
  52. Blizzards combine heavy snowfall or blowing snow with strong winds and very low visibility, turning familiar landscapes into disorienting white expanses where travel becomes
      dangerous and sometimes completely impossible.
  53. Stratocumulus clouds cover vast stretches of the subtropical oceans, forming lumpy gray sheets that reflect large amounts of sunlight back into space and play a surprisingly
      important role in cooling the entire planet.
  54. Heat lightning is simply ordinary lightning from a distant thunderstorm that is too far away for its thunder to be heard, often glimpsed as silent flickers illuminating clouds
      along the horizon on warm summer evenings.
  55. Weather forecasting relies on numerical models that divide the atmosphere into millions of grid cells, solving physical equations step by step to predict how temperature, wind,
      clouds, and precipitation will evolve.
  56. Arcus clouds, including both shelf clouds and roll clouds, are low horizontal formations associated with storm outflow, and the roll variety can even detach completely and
      appear to tumble slowly across the sky.
  57. Drizzle consists of very fine droplets falling from low stratus clouds, and although it rarely produces much accumulation, it can persist for hours and make an entire day feel
      damp, chilly, gray, and thoroughly dreary.
  58. Pyrocumulus clouds form above intense wildfires or volcanic eruptions, as the extreme heat drives powerful updrafts that carry smoke and moisture skyward, sometimes producing
      lightning that ignites even more new fires.
  59. Cloud classification dates back to Luke Howard, an English pharmacist who in 1803 proposed Latin names such as cumulus, stratus, and cirrus, establishing a system that
      meteorologists around the world still use today.
  60. Watching clouds drift and change across the sky remains one of the simplest pleasures in nature, offering both a quiet moment of reflection and a constantly shifting preview of
      the weather that tomorrow may bring.
